q: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view described in Text 1?

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Ito (Text 2) most likely respond to the gardeners' practice described in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Many home gardeners water their plants a little every day, believing that frequent watering keeps plants healthy.

Text 2
Horticulturist Ben Ito advises watering deeply but only once or twice a week. Shallow daily watering, he explains, encourages roots to stay near the surface, leaving plants vulnerable during dry spells, while deep watering encourages roots to grow downward.
c: He would say that shallow daily watering can actually weaken plants.
He would agree that plants need some water every day.
He would say that plants rarely need water at all.
He would recommend watering only in winter.
w: He recommends watering only once or twice a week.
He recommends deep watering, not none.
Seasons aren't discussed.
items.e: Ito explains that shallow daily watering keeps roots near the surface and leaves plants vulnerable.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Kim (Text 2) most likely respond to the teachers' argument in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Some teachers ban phones in class, arguing that the devices inevitably distract students from learning.

Text 2
Teacher Rosa Kim allows phones in her classroom, but only for specific tasks, such as looking up a word or photographing notes on the board. She found that once phones had a clear purpose, students rarely used them for games or messages.
c: She would suggest that phones need not be distracting when their use is clearly limited.
She would agree that phones should always be banned.
She would argue that games help students learn.
She would say students should use phones whenever they wish.
w: She allows phones for set tasks.
She found students rarely played games; she doesn't recommend them.
She limits phones to specific tasks.
items.e: Kim's experience challenges "inevitably": with clear limits, phones weren't a distraction.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Patel (Text 2) most likely respond to the city leaders' belief in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Some city leaders believe that building more parking garages downtown will bring shoppers back to struggling local stores.

Text 2
Planner Dev Patel studied downtowns that added large parking garages. He found that the number of shoppers changed little, while downtowns that instead widened sidewalks and added benches and trees saw noticeably more visitors.
c: He would doubt that adding parking alone would bring back shoppers.
He would agree that garages are the best way to attract shoppers.
He would argue that downtowns should ban all cars.
He would claim that shoppers prefer garages to sidewalks.
w: His data showed garages changed little.
He never proposes banning cars.
His findings suggest the opposite.
items.e: Patel found garages did little, while walkable improvements drew more visitors.

items.q: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
items.p:
Text 1
Reading aloud to young children builds their vocabulary, because children hear words they would rarely encounter in everyday conversation.

Text 2
Reading aloud does matter, but researcher Ama Owusu found that the largest vocabulary gains came when adults paused to talk with children about the story, asking questions and explaining unfamiliar words.
c: Reading aloud to young children can help build their vocabulary.
Talking about a story matters more than reading it.
Children learn no words from everyday conversation.
Reading aloud should be replaced by conversation.
w: Text 1 doesn't make this comparison.
Text 1 says children rarely hear such words in conversation, not that they learn none.
Text 2 says reading aloud matters.
items.e: Both texts accept that reading aloud helps vocabulary. Text 2 adds that discussion increases the gains.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Marsh (Text 2) most likely respond to the belief described in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
A popular belief holds that goldfish have extremely short memories, lasting only a few seconds.

Text 2
Biologist Leo Marsh trained goldfish to push a small lever to receive food, but only at a certain time of day. Months later, after the lever had been removed and then returned, the fish still gathered at it at the trained time.
c: He would say that his findings contradict the belief.
He would agree that goldfish forget within seconds.
He would say that goldfish cannot be trained.
He would claim that goldfish remember only colors.
w: His fish remembered for months.
He trained them successfully.
Colors weren't tested.
items.e: Remembering a trained behavior months later contradicts a memory of a few seconds.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Aziz (Text 2) most likely respond to the recommendation in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Some popular diet guides recommend avoiding all dietary fats in order to stay healthy.

Text 2
Dietitian Noor Aziz explains that the body needs certain fats, such as those found in nuts and fish, in order to absorb some vitamins. She recommends limiting some types of fat rather than eliminating fat from the diet entirely.
c: She would argue that avoiding all fats could be harmful.
She would fully endorse avoiding all fats.
She would say that vitamins are unnecessary.
She would recommend eating only nuts and fish.
w: She says the body needs some fats.
She says fats help the body absorb vitamins.
Nuts and fish are examples, not a whole diet.
items.e: Because some fats are needed to absorb vitamins, cutting out all fat could cause harm.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Ruiz (Text 2) most likely respond to the description in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Local histories often describe the town's first public library, which opened in 1902, as a gift from a single wealthy donor.

Text 2
Historian Clara Ruiz points out that the donor paid only for the library building. Town residents raised the money for books and staff themselves, through decades of bake sales, concerts, and small yearly subscriptions.
c: She would say that the description leaves out residents' major contributions.
She would agree that the donor funded everything.
She would argue that the library opened much earlier.
She would say that the donor opposed the library.
w: She shows residents funded books and staff.
The opening date isn't disputed.
The donor paid for the building.
items.e: Ruiz shows residents funded much of the library, which the single-donor story omits.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Brennan (Text 2) most likely respond to the economists' argument in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Many economists argue that raising the price of gasoline through taxes will lead people to drive less.

Text 2
Economist Hal Brennan found that in the short term, people drive about the same amount when gas prices rise, since commutes cannot easily change. Over several years, however, people buy more efficient cars and move closer to work, and total driving falls.
c: He would say that the effect described in Text 1 may take years to appear.
He would say that higher prices never affect driving.
He would say that driving falls immediately when prices rise.
He would argue that gas taxes should be lowered.
w: Driving falls over several years.
He found little short-term change.
He makes no policy recommendation.
items.e: Brennan agrees that driving falls, but only gradually, as people change cars and homes.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Cho (Text 2) most likely respond to the critics' praise in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Critics have praised photographer Mina Cho's portraits for capturing her subjects' true personalities.

Text 2
Cho herself is skeptical of such praise. A portrait, she says, shows only how a person looked during one second in front of a camera, often while feeling self-conscious, and it reveals as much about the photographer's choices as about the subject.
c: She would question whether a portrait can capture a subject's true personality.
She would agree that her portraits reveal true personalities.
She would argue that self-conscious subjects make better portraits.
She would say that photographers make no choices.
w: She is skeptical of that praise.
She mentions self-consciousness as a limitation.
She emphasizes the photographer's choices.
items.e: Cho says a portrait records one self-conscious moment shaped by the photographer, not a person's true self.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would the study's authors (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Bike-share programs reduce car traffic by giving people an easy alternative to driving for short trips.

Text 2
A study of one city's bike-share program found that most riders would otherwise have walked or taken a bus, not driven. The program still benefited riders by saving them time, the study's authors noted, but its effect on car traffic was small.
c: They would say the program's effect on car traffic may be smaller than claimed.
They would agree that bike-share greatly reduces car traffic.
They would say that bike-share has no benefits.
They would argue that buses should be eliminated.
w: They found the traffic effect was small.
They note riders saved time.
They make no recommendation about buses.
items.e: Most riders replaced walking or buses, not cars, so the effect on traffic was small.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Ndiaye (Text 2) most likely respond to the proposal in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Some scientists propose planting very large numbers of trees to slow climate change, since trees absorb carbon dioxide as they grow.

Text 2
Ecologist Ruth Ndiaye supports tree planting but warns that planting trees in grasslands that never had forests can harm species adapted to open land and may even reduce the amount of carbon stored in the soil.
c: She would support the idea but caution that where trees are planted matters.
She would reject tree planting entirely.
She would deny that trees absorb carbon dioxide.
She would recommend planting trees mainly in grasslands.
w: She supports tree planting.
She doesn't dispute this.
She warns against planting in natural grasslands.
items.e: Ndiaye supports planting but warns that planting in the wrong places can backfire.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Petrov (Text 2) most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Several older studies concluded that babies cannot recognize faces until they are several months old.

Text 2
Using newer equipment that precisely tracks where infants look, psychologist Ivan Petrov found that newborns only a few days old look longer at face-like patterns than at other shapes with the same brightness and size.
c: He would say that newer methods suggest the ability may begin earlier than the older studies concluded.
He would agree that recognition begins only after several months.
He would argue that newborns cannot see shapes.
He would say that brightness explains the newborns' behavior.
w: His newborns already preferred faces.
They distinguished face-like patterns.
He controlled for brightness.
items.e: Petrov's newborn data challenge the older conclusion, and better methods are the likely reason.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would the researchers (Text 2) most likely respond to the assumption in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Many people assume that working from home reduces collaboration among coworkers.

Text 2
Researchers at a design firm compared teams before and after a shift to remote work. Scheduled meetings stayed about as frequent as before, but brief, unplanned conversations dropped sharply, and employees reported fewer new ideas arising from chance encounters.
c: They would partly agree, noting that informal interactions declined even though scheduled ones did not.
They would completely disagree, since meetings stayed frequent.
They would argue that remote work improved collaboration.
They would say that nothing changed after the shift.
w: Informal conversations dropped sharply.
Nothing suggests improvement.
Unplanned conversations dropped.
items.e: Their finding is mixed: formal collaboration held steady, but informal collaboration fell.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Morin (Text 2) most likely respond to the view in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
A popular view holds that the ancient city of Varo was abandoned suddenly after an earthquake struck the region.

Text 2
Archaeologist Tess Morin notes that houses in Varo were emptied of valuables and their doors carefully sealed, and that the most recent coins found in the city date from decades before the earthquake.
c: She would argue that the city was likely abandoned gradually and deliberately before the earthquake.
She would agree that people fled the moment the earthquake struck.
She would say that the earthquake never happened.
She would claim that the city was never inhabited.
w: Sealed, emptied houses suggest planning, not panic.
She dates the evidence relative to the earthquake rather than denying it.
The houses and coins show people lived there.
items.e: Emptied, sealed houses and coins from decades earlier point to planned abandonment before the quake.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Brooks (Text 2) most likely respond to the scholars' reading in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Some literary scholars read the poet's final collection as an expression of despair, pointing to its many images of winter and darkness.

Text 2
Scholar Imani Brooks notes that nearly every winter image in the collection is paired with a sign of return, such as buds beneath snow or a lamp lit at dusk. Read as a whole, she argues, the collection is less about loss than about endurance.
c: She would argue that the scholars overlook how the dark images are balanced by signs of renewal.
She would agree that the collection mainly expresses despair.
She would say that the poems contain no images of winter.
She would argue that the collection is about spring rather than endurance.
w: She reads the collection as about endurance.
She acknowledges the winter images.
She calls it about endurance, not spring.
items.e: Brooks accepts that the winter imagery is there but shows it is paired with renewal, so the scholars' reading is incomplete.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Venn (Text 2) most likely respond to the proponents' argument in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Proponents of standardized admissions tests argue that the tests provide an objective measure that lets colleges compare students from very different high schools.

Text 2
Researcher Paul Venn agrees that a common measure is useful, but he found that at many colleges, high school grades predicted first-year success about as well as test scores did, and that combining the two predicted best of all.
c: He would accept the value of a common measure but suggest that tests are most useful alongside grades.
He would argue that tests should replace grades entirely.
He would reject comparing students from different schools.
He would claim that grades are useless for predicting success.
w: Grades predicted about as well, and combining the two was best.
He calls a common measure useful.
Grades predicted well in his data.
items.e: Venn agrees in part (a common measure helps) but found grades and scores together predicted best.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Varga (Text 2) most likely respond to the historians' view in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Historians have often credited the invention of the printing press with rapidly spreading literacy across Europe.

Text 2
Historian Elena Varga observes that in many regions, literacy rates rose only slowly for two centuries after printing presses arrived, increasing sharply only when schooling became widely available.
c: She would argue that printing alone may not explain the rise in literacy, which depended heavily on schooling.
She would agree that printing caused literacy to spread rapidly.
She would claim that printing presses arrived only recently.
She would argue that schooling reduced literacy.
w: She found literacy rose slowly after printing.
She says presses arrived two centuries before the sharp rise.
Literacy rose with schooling.
items.e: Varga links the sharp rise in literacy to schooling, not to printing alone.

items.q: Based on the texts, how would Lund (Text 2) most likely respond to the view in Text 1?
items.p:
Text 1
Many zoologists hold that animals raised in captivity lose the hunting skills of their wild relatives.

Text 2
In a study by zoologist Kai Lund, captive-born otters released into a large enclosure stocked with live fish caught prey within days, though less efficiently than wild otters at first. After a month, the difference had largely disappeared.
c: He would suggest that such skills may be dormant rather than lost and can recover quickly.
He would agree that captive animals permanently lose hunting skills.
He would argue that captive otters hunt better than wild ones.
He would say that otters do not hunt fish.
w: The otters caught up within a month.
They were less efficient at first and only caught up later.
The otters caught fish.
items.e: The otters were weaker at first but caught up within a month, which suggests the skills were dormant, not lost.
